extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of literary criticism; poetry readers and teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate poems and critical responses with attention to 'sincerity' (various senses), to whether technical features serve the whole, and to avoiding unexamined preconceptions about what poetry must do. Focus is on close-reading criteria and critical method rather than prescriptive metre/forme rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity (central critical virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity is the quality critics and poetry most insistently require; it is a necessary virtue in both poem and critic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards treats sincerity as multifaceted and essential to good poetry and good criticism; he argues critics should seek tests for sincerity, cultivate it in themselves, and not take it for granted. Sincerity fluctuates with health, company, responsibility, and proximity to the object; bogus forms (confident assurance, rootless convictions) may masquerade as sincerity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish emotional acceptance from intellectual assent
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotional acceptance (our response) can be separate from intellectual conviction; we may give emotional assent without intellectual belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic should recognize the two forms of belief and not confuse them; many poems request emotional assent without providing intellectual proof, and this is not necessarily insincere. Richards argues the same solution for minor cases applies to major philosophical/religious problems in poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insincerity as discrepancy between poem’s claim and poet’s shaping impulses
rubrics_metrics.description: Insincerity occurs where there is a discrepancy between what a poem claims upon our response and the shaping impulses in the poet’s mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the poet’s shaping impulses are relevant; the reader should attempt to detect whether a poem’s asserted emotional claim is grounded in the poet’s genuine shaping motives. Examples: works written to appear original/striking often show this discrepancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial motive acceptable if it doesn’t interfere with growth
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem can be written for money, pique, or ambition and still be good, provided these external motives do not interfere with its growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards explicitly allows non-ideal motives so long as they do not obstruct the organic development of the poem. Interference (e.g., forced originality) is the real problem, not the mere presence of extrinsic motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interferences that cause insincerity (anti-patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain motives and deliberate effects—especially desire to be ‘original’, ‘striking’, or ‘poetic’—are usual causes of insincerity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should watch for signs that these desires have distorted the poem’s organic shaping impulses. Such interferences are a primary source of insincerity in poems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irony is not necessarily insincere
rubrics_metrics.description: Irony—where the overtly professed feeling may be the opposite of the feeling present—is not necessarily insincere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of irony should not be equated with insincerity; the critic must examine shaping impulses and context rather than assuming irony = false feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity as ideal ‘perfect-mind’ standard (benchmark of genuineness)
rubrics_metrics.description: One sense of sincerity is the product a perfect mind would produce—free from impurities or interfering impulses; this is an ideal standard for measuring degrees of insincerity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards notes this is mostly a theoretical ideal useful only to measure relative insincerity; perfect-mind sincerity is unattainable but serves as a yardstick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity as simplicity/spontaneity (appearance of naturalness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A common sense of sincerity is that a feeling is genuine if left in its natural state, not worked over—spontaneous rather than sophisticated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sense is common but risky: apparent spontaneity can be the result of cultivated self-control; simplicity may be valued too uncritically. Richards warns this sense is of limited use in criticism because such raw spontaneity is rare and may be illusory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity as self-completion/inner-order (Confucian sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity may be understood as self-completion or inner order: the tendency of the mind toward a more perfect, harmonious organization that unites internal and external.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawing on Chung Yung, Richards suggests this practical sense allows intuition (hitting what is right without effort) for those who have attained it, while enabling them to recognize when more study is needed. This sense provides a usable standard and suggests ways to promote sincerity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity is shown by responses that embody inner adjustment tendency
rubrics_metrics.description: Any response which embodies the present activity of the tendency to inner adjustment is sincere; responses that conflict with or inhibit that tendency are insincere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, critics should look for responses that appear to spring from an ordered, experience-linked mind rather than from confusion, fixed prejudice, or misplaced emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test sincerity by comparison with responses ‘beyond suspicion’
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge a new response whose sincerity is doubtful, compare it with those responses we know to be beyond suspicion (e.g., reflexive dislikes like hating a bad smell) and use them as standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards recommends using clearly reliable, simple responses as instruments to extend and check sincerity in less certain fields; this is a method for critics to ground uncertain judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques/rituals to heighten sincerity (provocations to test responses)
rubrics_metrics.description: When unsure whether a poem’s effects are genuinely ours, consider it in a frame of feelings whose sincerity is beyond question: contemplate loneliness, birth/death, universe’s immensity, enormity of ignorance, and man’s place in time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards suggests meditative practices and analogous rituals (religious exercises, divination practices) as ways to supply standards for testing whether our reactions are deep, genuine, and not fashion or surface response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity cannot be willed into existence (anti-method)
rubrics_metrics.description: A direct effort to be sincere, like other efforts to will oneself into action, usually frustrates its intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should not attempt mere volitional fixes; instead, cultivate conditions that encourage inner order and allow sincerity to arise naturally (study, comparison, reflection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the fluctuating, fallible nature of critics’ sincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity in critics varies with health, companions, responsibility, nearness to object; critics can feel sincere when they are not and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics must be self-aware and humble, using methods (further study, comparison, ritual) to check their responses rather than assuming infallibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Technical Presupposition Fallacy (judging means apart from ends)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not suppose that the means a poet uses are valuable for their own sake or that they can be prescribed without reference to the poet’s aim; details must be judged with reference to the whole final result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a principal methodological warning: critics should not assign independent marks to details (rhyme, metre, etc.) without considering how they serve the poem’s overall effect or purpose. Richards calls this blunder extremely insidious and gives many examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish means from ends in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful to decide whether a reader’s demand concerns means (technical devices) or ends (the result/value); the verb ‘to say’ in poetry is ambiguous between ‘communicate’ and ‘state’.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards urges critics to clarify whether a judgment is about technique or overall value; many confusions and misapplied prescriptions stem from failing to make this distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfect rhymes: not intrinsically bad
rubrics_metrics.description: Imperfect rhymes (and metrical irregularities) should not be condemned automatically as defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a common occasion for folly; such features must be judged by their contribution to the whole poem, not by a dogmatic rule that rhymes must be perfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrical irregularities: judged by effect, not rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Metrical irregularities are legitimate or flawed depending on how they function within the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards lists metrical irregularities among technical presuppositions often misapplied; locate their role in the larger pattern before condemning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line-end stop (caesura/pause): context-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: The Line-end Stop is not inherently correct or incorrect; its value depends on the poem’s overall movement and intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid applying a rigid rule about line-end stops; treat this formal device as part of the poem’s means, to be assessed by the end it serves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sonnet form: form is not an automatic standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Sonnets need not have a fixed, prescriptive division; sonnet-form expectations should not override consideration of the poem’s aims and effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards includes Sonnet Form among items critics fetishize; the particular use of sonnet conventions must be read in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cacophony and euphony: evaluate by appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Cacophony and euphony are intrinsic sound qualities but their value depends on whether the poem requires them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards lists Cacophony and Euphony as technical details often misused as absolute criteria; judge whether the sound matches the poem’s needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic qualities of words: beware reification
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid treating the 'intrinsic qualities' of words (as if words carry fixed virtues) as independent guarantees of poetic value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics often shorthand their experience (saying 'the poem has beauty' instead of describing effects); this invites the reification of word-qualities separate from their effect on readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive accuracy: verify fit to poem’s aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Demands for strict descriptive accuracy should be applied only insofar as they serve the poem’s end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive accuracy is listed among technical presuppositions that can mislead; sometimes poetic truth differs from factual exactness in service of higher aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vividness: contextually justified virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Vividness is valuable when required by the poem’s aims, not as an automatic measure of worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vividness appears among features often demanded independently; Richards warns that craving vividness can blind readers to subtler values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic: apply where poem intends logical coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Logical consistency is desirable when the poem’s aims require it, but logic is not a universal litmus test for poetic value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a technical presupposition—beware insisting on logic where the poem’s mode is associative, imagistic, or otherwise non-discursive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unmixed metaphor and figurative language conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Demands for unmixed metaphor and conventional figurative neatness must be weighed against the poem’s purposes; they are not absolute rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards references problems of figurative language and unmixed metaphor as frequently enunciated dogmas; critics should test these against overall result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and Conciseness: borderline technical presuppositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Insistence upon Clarity and Conciseness may be misplaced depending on poetic aims; these are sometimes debatable technical presuppositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards notes greater doubt about absolute insistence on clarity/conciseness; they may be desirable but are not universal goods for all poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majesty in epitaphs (genre-specific demand)
rubrics_metrics.description: A demand that epitaphs possess majesty is a genre-specific expectation and should be treated as such, not as a universal standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards lists 'Majesty in Epitaphs' as an example where a technical presupposition pertains to genre and should be evaluated accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serious subject/message (subject-theory) is not sole value test
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory that the value of poetry resides in the value of its subject (or in an inspiring message) is a reflective preconception that can be tested and found wanting when applied as a direct criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards shows how subject- or message-based judgments lead to crude conclusions (e.g., judging a poem good/ bad merely by whether its subject is important). He compares this to lilt-theory: such single-factor tests blind readers to other values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lilt (musicality) is not an independent test of value
rubrics_metrics.description: Lilt or musical ease is fine when the poem requires it, but it cannot be applied independently as a test of poetic value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards warns that quests for lilt can render readers insensitive to other movements and values in a poem; treat musical qualities as conditioned by the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test critical theories by their serviceability in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: General preconceptions (theories about poetry’s value) should be judged by whether they are described in a way directly serviceable in critical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a theory of value permits easy, direct application to judgments (e.g., subject-theory), it is suspect; the more refined a preconception, the less likely it is directly applicable without distortion.
